demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette:
Kealani sits in the waiting room, her large, capable hands resting motionless in her lap. For forty years, those hands have opened doors, checked locks, and guided people to safety. Now, they feel like foreign objects, the hands of a stranger. At sixty-one, she had believed the quiet, predictable rhythm of her life was set. She worked the graveyard shift as a security guard at the local university, a job she took pride in. The silent, empty campus at 3 a.m. was her domain, a place of order she helped maintain. That sense of order shattered nine months ago on a rain-slicked service road behind the chemistry building.

The memory, when it comes, is not a flood but a series of disjointed, sterile images. She can recall the squawk of the radio reporting a tripped alarm and the slightly-too-fast speed of her electric patrol cart as she rounded the blind corner by the loading dock. She remembers the squeal of the tires on the wet asphalt. Then there is a gap, a silent, black space that her mind refuses to fill. The next image is of the young man, a graduate student, on the ground, his leg bent at an impossible angle. She remembers looking at him, then at her own hands on the steering wheel, and feeling a profound and terrifying disconnect, as if she were watching a poorly edited film about someone else’s horrible mistake. When she is forced to recount the event for reports, the words come out flat, devoid of the horror she feels she is supposed to perform. This numbness scares her more than tears would; it feels like proof of some fundamental rot within her.

In the months since, Kealani’s mind has become a prison of looping thoughts. She spends her nights off, and increasingly her time on patrol, going over and over the few seconds before the impact. She dissects every detail she can grasp: her speed, the low visibility, the dark clothing the student was wearing. She is searching for a key, a single piece of information that will make the senseless event finally click into place, to make it make sense. But it never does. The analysis always dissolves into a bitter tide of self-blame. She dwells relentlessly on what she did wrong, the hundred tiny ways she could have averted the disaster. If she had just taken the corner a little wider, if she had paused for a second longer, if she hadn’t been so focused on the call. Each "if only" is a fresh indictment of her failure.

This relentless internal prosecution has bled into a larger, more agonizing question: why her? She finds herself staring at the ceiling in the dark, trying to understand what this event means for her life, for who she is. After a lifetime of trying to be a good, careful person, why was she chosen to be the agent of such pain? It feels like a cosmic punishment, a verdict on her character delivered in the cruelest possible way. Her work, once a source of quiet pride, is now a landscape of constant threat. The corner by the chemistry building is a place she can barely force herself to drive past, her body rigid, her eyes scanning the shadows for threats that are no longer there. Her patrol times have slowed, and her supervisor has noticed.

She has pulled away from her small circle of friends, convinced she is tainted. How can she share a laugh over coffee when she carries the weight of what she did? The memory feels like it belongs to a monster, and she has come to believe that monster is her. It was after a particularly bad night, spent circling the campus in a state of near-paralysis, that she finally made the call. She is here now not because she believes she can be fixed, but because the exhaustion of re-living, re-analysing, and re-condemning herself every single day has become unbearable. She is terrified that therapy will only confirm her deepest fear—that she is as negligent and broken as she feels—but the sliver of hope that she might one day feel like herself again is, for now, just enough to keep her in the chair.
